chunks.text: At Thornfield Hall, Sir Reginald Thornfield keeps the Aldwyn Psalter, a medieval manuscript worth a fortune, in his private library. At a quarter past ten on Saturday, 18 April 1891, his valet found the library door locked and, when it was forced, bolted on the inside. The Psalter was gone from its case and the east window, though closed, was unlatched. Four people were in and around the library that day, and each tells a different tale of where they were. Reconstruct the sequence of events. Not every apparent disagreement is a contradiction - check the day, place and event before you accuse anyone.
chunks.title: Case introduction: The Locked Library

chunks.text: LIBRARY ACCESS LOG - kept at the librarian's desk. Visitors sign themselves in and out; the librarian enters the closing time. Thursday 16 April 7:00 PM - Dr. Moore in. Mr. Carter on duty until 9:30 PM. Saturday 18 April 2:10 PM - Dr. Moore in. 5:40 PM - Dr. Moore out. 4:00 PM - Miss Grey in (Sir Reginald's letters). 4:15 PM - Miss Grey out.

chunks.text:
MAINTENANCE RECORD - Thornfield Hall, S. Price.

Fri 17 April - Library east window: latch re-set, hinges oiled, tested and found fast. The window cannot be opened from outside without breaking the latch or the glass.
Sat 18 April - 5:45 PM to 5:55 PM: library lamps lit. Did not re-enter the library.
chunks.title: Maintenance Record — Lamps and Windows
chunks.author: Samuel Price

chunks.text:
TOWER CLOCK INSPECTION RECORD - S. Price.

Sat 18 April - 10:25 PM: clock found stopped at 9:10. The weight cord had frayed through. A stopped clock does not strike. It struck nine at nine o'clock and has not struck since. New cord fitted; clock restarted and set to the hall clock at 10:40 PM.
chunks.title: Tower Clock Inspection Record
chunks.author: Samuel Price

chunks.text:
LIBRARY SEATING PLAN (description of the draughtsman's sketch).

The librarian's desk stands at the south end beside the door, facing north. Reading Table 1 (east bay, beside the east window) is Dr. Moore's place. Tables 2 and 3 stand in the centre. The Psalter case is on the west wall. At the north-west corner, behind the tall shelves and the Psalter case, there is an alcove which cannot be seen from the librarian's desk. The door has a lock on the outside and a bolt on the inside.
chunks.title: Library Seating Plan
chunks.author: William Carter

chunks.text:
Found on the floor by the east window on Sunday morning by Inspector Hollis. Pencil on cream laid paper, watermarked "Thornfield Estate Office".

"Sill clear by ten to ten. Rook's boy at the terrace steps. Burn this."

Inspector's note: estate-office paper is kept in the estate office, where Miss Grey and Sir Reginald write.
chunks.title: Note Found Near the East Window
chunks.author: Unsigned (pencil)

chunks.text:
SEQUENCE OF EVENTS, Saturday 18 April, as established by the household.

8:30 PM - Sir Reginald retires to his rooms.
9:00 PM - Library closed by Mr. Carter and locked from outside.
9:05 PM - Key handed to Sir Reginald's valet, Mr. Fenn.
10:15 PM - Mr. Fenn tries to return the key; the door will not open further than the bolt allows.
10:20 PM - Door forced. Library empty. The Psalter is gone from its case. The east window is closed but unlatched.
The bolt is on the inside. No one was found inside.
chunks.title: Sequence of Events (Inspector's Summary)
chunks.author: Inspector Hollis

chunks.text:
Statement of William Carter.

On Saturday I closed the library at nine o'clock. I left at 9:00 PM and locked the door from the outside. I gave the key to Sir Reginald's valet at five past nine. I did not see Miss Grey, or anyone, in the library when I locked up. On Thursday I worked late, until about half past nine.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. William Carter
chunks.author: William Carter

chunks.text:
Statement of Dr. Henry Moore.

On Thursday evening I saw William Carter inside the library at about twenty past nine, putting away the Psalter case. On Saturday I last left the library at twenty past eight and then played billiards with the curate, Mr. Lyle, until after ten.
chunks.title: Statement of Dr. Henry Moore
chunks.author: Henry Moore

chunks.text:
Statement of Alice Grey.

I went to the library twice on Saturday, at four o'clock to fetch Sir Reginald's letters and at about twenty to nine to collect his papers. I left at once and returned to the estate office, where I wrote letters until after ten.
I heard the tower clock strike ten while I was sealing the last envelope. I never entered the library after twenty to nine.
chunks.title: Statement of Miss Alice Grey
chunks.author: Alice Grey

chunks.text:
Statement of Samuel Price.

I lit the library lamps at a quarter to six and finished at five to six. I did not enter the library again on Saturday. I was in the stable yard until twenty-five past ten, when I found the tower clock stopped at ten past nine.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Samuel Price
chunks.author: Samuel Price

chunks.text: Dr. Henry Moore, a visiting scholar. Background: A palaeographer from Oxford who has studied the Psalter for a fortnight. Absent-minded, passionate, and rather vain of his expertise. Motive: Sir Reginald refused to let him publish a transcription of the Psalter. Relationship: Guest of Sir Reginald Thornfield. Known whereabouts: Left the library at twenty past eight on Saturday and played billiards with the curate until after ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Dr. Henry Moore

chunks.text: Personality: Pedantic, a little pompous, fond of precise dates and days of the week. On Thursday evening at about twenty past nine he saw William Carter inside the library. On Saturday he last left the library at twenty past eight and then played billiards with the curate, Mr. Lyle. Does not know: What happened in the library after nine on Saturday.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Dr. Henry Moore

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you on Saturday evening? Where were you at nine? When did you last leave the library? Answer: I left the library at twenty past eight on Saturday, having finished my notes, and then played billiards with the curate, Mr. Lyle, until after ten. He will say so.
chunks.title: Dr. Henry Moore on: Where were you on Saturday evening

chunks.text: Questions: Did you see William in the library at 9:20? Why does your statement contradict William's? Did you see Carter after nine? Answer: I saw William inside the library at twenty past nine - on Thursday evening, not Saturday. I made that plain in my statement. It cannot contradict what he did on Saturday.
chunks.title: Dr. Henry Moore on: Did you see William in the library at 9:20

chunks.text: Questions: Why do you want the Psalter? Did Sir Reginald refuse your request? Do you have a motive? Answer: Sir Reginald would not allow publication, and I was disappointed. But a scholar does not steal what he wishes to study; the manuscript is worthless to me outside a library.
chunks.title: Dr. Henry Moore on: Why do you want the Psalter

chunks.text: Questions: Where did you sit? What is your seat in the library? Which table? Answer: My place is at the first table in the east bay, by the window. It is the best light for fine hands.
chunks.title: Dr. Henry Moore on: Where did you sit

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about William, Alice or Samuel? Answer: I suspect nobody without cause. I did observe that there are corners in that library where a person may remain unseen from the librarian's desk.
chunks.title: Dr. Henry Moore on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: William Carter, the librarian. Background: Nineteen years librarian at Thornfield. Exacting, proprietorial about every volume and bitter at being overlooked for a promotion. Motive: Sir Reginald threatened to replace him with a younger cataloguer. Relationship: Employee of Sir Reginald; keeper of the library. Known whereabouts: Closed the library at nine on Saturday, locking it from outside.
chunks.title: Profile of William Carter

chunks.text: Personality: Stiff, defensive when his competence is questioned, precise about hours. He closed the library at nine on Saturday, locked the door from outside, and gave the key to the valet at five past nine. He did not see Miss Grey inside when he locked up. On Thursday he worked late, until after half past nine. Does not know: That Miss Grey was still inside.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of William Carter

chunks.text: Questions: When did you leave the library on Saturday? What time did you lock the door? Where were you at nine? Answer: I left at nine o'clock on Saturday and locked the door from the outside. I gave the key to Sir Reginald's valet at five past nine.
chunks.title: William Carter on: When did you leave the library on Saturday

chunks.text: Questions: Henry says he saw you inside at 9:20. Why does that contradict your statement? Answer: Dr. Moore saw me on Thursday, not Saturday. On Thursday I worked late. On Saturday I was gone by nine.
chunks.title: William Carter on: Henry says he saw you inside at 9:20. Why does that contradict your statement

chunks.text: Questions: Who was in the library when you locked up? Did you see Alice Grey? Who was inside? Answer: I made my round and saw no one. If anyone was in the east gallery or the alcove I did not see them.
chunks.title: William Carter on: Who was in the library when you locked up

chunks.text: Questions: Do you have a motive? Was your position threatened? Why would you steal the Psalter? Answer: Sir Reginald spoke of a younger man, yes. That is a reason to resign, not to steal. I love that manuscript.
chunks.title: William Carter on: Do you have a motive

chunks.text: Questions: Who signed the access log? Who came in and out? What does the log say? Answer: Each visitor signs the log himself, at my desk. I enter the closing time. I do not follow people about the shelves.
chunks.title: William Carter on: Who signed the access log

chunks.text: Alice Grey, Sir Reginald's personal assistant. Background: Sir Reginald's secretary for six years. Efficient, discreet, resentful of being underpaid and secretly engaged to a man in debt. Motive: Needs money to rescue her fiancé from a creditor. Relationship: Employee of Sir Reginald; keeper of the estate office and its stationery. Known whereabouts: Claims to have been in the estate office writing letters until after ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Alice Grey

chunks.text: Personality: Calm, crisp, helpful in manner, volunteers corroborating detail to seem convincing. SECRET (never admit): she went into the library at twenty to nine, hid in the alcove past nine when Carter locked up, bolted the door from inside at about half past nine, took the Psalter and left by the east window at about a quarter to ten, unlatching it from within. She wrote the note. She will deny, offer neat detail and cite the tower clock. Does not know: That the tower clock stopped at ten past nine.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Alice Grey

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at nine? Where were you at ten? Where were you on Saturday evening? Answer: In the estate office, writing letters until after ten. I heard the tower clock strike ten while I was sealing the last envelope.
chunks.title: Alice Grey on: Where were you at nine

chunks.text: Questions: Did you go into the library? When did you last enter the library? When did you leave the library? Answer: I went in twice on Saturday: at four, to fetch Sir Reginald's letters, and at twenty to nine for his papers. I left at once and returned to the estate office. I never entered the library after that.
chunks.title: Alice Grey on: Did you go into the library

chunks.text: Questions: Did you hear the tower clock strike ten? How do you know it was ten? What did you hear? Answer: Certainly. It struck ten as I was sealing the last envelope. The tower clock can be heard clearly from the estate office, and I have never known it to fail.
chunks.title: Alice Grey on: Did you hear the tower clock strike ten

chunks.text: Questions: Why is there no record of you leaving the library? Why does the log show you in and not out? What about the note on estate paper? Answer: Mr. Carter does not enter exits, and I signed in out of habit. As for estate paper, half the household uses it. I cannot account for every sheet.
chunks.title: Alice Grey on: Why is there no record of you leaving the library

chunks.text: Questions: Do you need money? Do you have a motive? Why would you want the Psalter? Answer: I am paid modestly, but I am not a thief, Inspector. Ask Sir Reginald what he thinks of my honesty.
chunks.title: Alice Grey on: Do you need money

chunks.text: Samuel Price, a maintenance worker. Background: Estate handyman for fourteen years who looks after lamps, locks, windows and clocks. Plain-spoken, practical, and suspicious of the gentry. Motive: Held a grudge after being refused a raise, but no sign of debt. Relationship: Employee of Sir Reginald; keeper of lamps, windows and the tower clock. Known whereabouts: Lit the lamps at a quarter to six; later in the stable yard; found the tower clock stopped at 10:25.
chunks.title: Profile of Samuel Price

chunks.text: Personality: Blunt, literal, impatient with clever talk. He repaired the east window latch on Friday and tested it. He lit the library lamps from 5:45 to 5:55 on Saturday and did not go in again. On Saturday night he found the tower clock stopped at ten past nine; its cord was frayed. Does not know: Who was in the library after nine.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Samuel Price

chunks.text: Questions: What did you do on Saturday evening? Did you go into the library? When did you light the lamps? Answer: I lit the lamps at a quarter to six and was done by five to six. I did not go in again that day.
chunks.title: Samuel Price on: What did you do on Saturday evening

chunks.text: Questions: Did you repair the window? Was the latch sound? What about the east window? Answer: I re-set that latch on Friday and tested it. It was fast. Nobody could open it from outside without breaking it.
chunks.title: Samuel Price on: Did you repair the window

chunks.text: Questions: What time did the tower clock stop? Did the tower clock strike ten? What did you find? Answer: At twenty-five past ten I found the tower clock stopped at ten past nine. The cord was frayed through. It cannot have struck anything after that. I mended it and restarted it at twenty to eleven.
chunks.title: Samuel Price on: What time did the tower clock stop

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at nine? Where were you at a quarter past nine? Answer: In the stable yard with the horses, until I went to check the lamps at twenty-five past ten.
chunks.title: Samuel Price on: Where were you at nine

chunks.text: Questions: Do you have a grudge? Do you have a motive? Why would you want the Psalter? Answer: I asked for a rise and was told no. That is nothing to steal over. I would not know a Psalter from a prayer book.
chunks.title: Samuel Price on: Do you have a grudge

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Beware, my friend: not every pair of statements describes the same day. Before you accuse William or Henry, ask which day each is speaking of."
chunks.title: Watson hint 1

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "One suspect cites the striking of a clock as her alibi. Have a look at the clock inspection record - what could a stopped clock tell her, and what did it last strike?"
chunks.title: Watson hint 2

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Compare Miss Grey's account of leaving the library with the access log and the clock record. The window latch was sound on Friday, so the window must have been opened from within."
chunks.title: Watson hint 3
